issues.legal_issue: A magistrate designated to hear a municipal claim for recovery is not an inferior criminal court when conducting the statutory recovery proceeding.
material_facts: The municipal body carried out repairs after the property owner failed to comply with a repair requisition and demanded the repair costs from the owner.
The municipal body applied to a magistrate designated to recover the amount through the statutory recovery process.
The owner challenged the magistrate’s recovery order by criminal revision.
The governing scheme allowed an appeal against the municipal demand, and the magistrate’s inquiry in the recovery proceeding was limited to recovery.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate acted as a persona designata in a recovery proceeding, not as an inferior criminal court; the criminal revision was therefore incompetent.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 222(4), 93 and 226 of the Ajmer-Merwara Municipalities Regulation, the repair costs treated as a tax could be challenged by appeal, leaving the proceeding under section 234 as a limited recovery proceeding. The designated magistrate acts as a persona designata, not as a criminal court exercising authority under the Code of Criminal Procedure, so the order is not revisable under section 439 of that Code. The Court rejected the contrary view in Crown through Municipal Committee, Ajmer v. Amba Lal and referred to Re Dinbai Jijibhai Khambatta, V. B. D’Monte v. Bandra Borough Municipality, Emperor v. Devappa Ramappa, Re Dalsukhram Hurgovandas and Municipal Committee, Lashkar v. Shahbuddin as examples of differing decisions on analogous provisions, without expressing an opinion on their correctness.

predicates.municipal_claim_recovery_proceeding: A municipal body seeks recovery of a claim through a statutory recovery proceeding.
predicates.magistrate_designated_to_handle_recovery: A magistrate hears the recovery application because the governing scheme designates that magistrate for the task.
predicates.criminal_revision_challenges_recovery_or: The claimant against whom recovery is sought challenges the magistrate’s recovery order by criminal revision.

issues.definition: When a designated magistrate handles a municipal recovery proceeding and the resulting order is challenged by criminal revision, the order is not treated as one of an inferior criminal court.

issues.legal_issue: Treating municipal repair costs as recoverable as a tax also makes the demand appealable under the statutory tax-appeal process.
material_facts: The municipal body’s repair costs became recoverable from the property owner as if they were a tax levied on the property.
The statutory scheme provided an appeal against the assessment or levy of a tax and contemplated appeals from orders of the kind made for recovering the repair costs.
issues.conclusion: An appeal under the statutory tax-appeal process lies against the municipal demand for the repair costs.
issues.legal_principle: Section 222(4) treats the amount recoverable for municipal work as if it were a tax levied on the property. The legal fiction must be given full effect: the tax-recovery procedure is available to the municipal body, and the taxpayer’s appeal right under section 93(1) is available as well. Section 226 confirms that orders of the relevant kind are appealable by providing for suspension of enforcement while an appeal is pending.

predicates.municipal_repair_cost_demand: A municipal body demands payment of costs it incurred carrying out repairs to property.
predicates.repair_costs_treated_as_property_tax: The governing scheme treats those repair costs as a tax levied on the property for recovery purposes.
predicates.statutory_tax_appeal_available: The governing scheme provides an appeal against the assessment or levy of a tax.

issues.definition: A repair-cost demand treated as a property tax is appealable through the available tax-appeal process.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of rules prescribing the form of a municipal demand does not make an otherwise claimable repair cost unenforceable.
material_facts: The owner did not carry out repairs after receiving the municipal requisition and subsequent notice that the municipal body would perform the work at the owner’s expense.
The municipal body performed the repairs and demanded reimbursement of the cost.
No rules had been framed prescribing the form for making the demand.
issues.conclusion: The absence of prescribed rules or a prescribed demand form does not prevent the municipal body from making the demand or seeking recovery of the repair costs.
issues.legal_principle: The absence of rules prescribing the form of a demand notice means only that no particular form has been prescribed. It does not nullify the statutory power to demand payment or render unenforceable an amount that is otherwise claimable. The Court also held that this merits contention could not be raised in a criminal revision that was incompetent.

rule.if: municipal_repair_cost_claim and owner_failed_to_make_required_repairs and municipal_body_completed_repairs_at_owner_expense and demand_form_rules_absent

predicates.municipal_repair_cost_claim: A municipal body claims reimbursement for costs associated with required repairs to property.
predicates.owner_failed_to_make_required_repairs: The property owner did not carry out repairs required by the municipal body.
predicates.municipal_body_completed_repairs_at_owne: The municipal body carried out the repairs and charged their cost to the owner.
predicates.demand_form_rules_absent: No rules prescribing the form of the payment demand had been made.

issues.definition: When an owner fails to make required repairs, the municipal body performs them at the owner’s expense, and no demand-form rules exist, the repair-cost demand remains enforceable.
